utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Gerry Dobbyn and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any preliminary matters before the witness is brought back in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, I just wanted to advise the Court of one thing: The Defence has filed an application for a binding order pursuant to Rule 54 bis and I wanted to indicate the Prosecution did not intend to file a written response. Our position is the same as it was to an earlier application to Croatia, I think this one is to the Federation, and I would only note that the request for information includes requests for information about unknown persons, FNU, LNU, first name unknown, last name unknown. We think that's unnecessary and an impossible thing to ask of the country to whom a request for a binding order is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted, Mr. Hannis. Thank you. Would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, good morning to you, sir. Before I invite Mr. Zecevic to continue, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, yesterday, before the very end, we discussed the events of late August 1992. Mr. Andan, sir, on the 28th of August, 1992, did you return all items that were issued to you, all items and equipment that were issued to you by the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was at my request; I wanted to have this hand-over of all the items that I was -- that I had been issued, the items that were necessary for my work and that were issued by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D348 MFI. That's under tab 141.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Andan --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be -- could the usher please assist with providing this binder to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request: Could the microphones, the witness's microphones, please be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So for you, witness, that's tab 141.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The microphones should not touch each other, could you please set them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report dated 31st of August, 1992, and it is entitled "The Commission Investigating the Allegations in the Petition by the Employees of the SJB Bijeljina." And then on the fourth page we can see the signatures of members of the commission, the Goran Macar, Sreto, and Spasojevic, Zoran. And then in paragraph 1 -- I've just lost the document. And then in paragraph 1 it says the minister of the interior issued a decision setting up a commission to verify the allegations in the petition by employees of the Bijeljina SJB. The commission was composed -- is -- shall be composed of Goran Macar, chairman of the commission; Sreto Gajic; and Zoran Spasojevic. Mr. Andan, were you aware that this commission was set up and that they were trying to establish certain facts about -- pursuant to some allegation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mention is made here of a petition by employees of the SJB of Bijeljina. Petition number 653/92 of 30th August, 1992. Do you know what this is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to see this commission report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think I've seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this commission report in any way -- did it involve you in any way and I mean did it involve you in view of the fact that there were certain allegations there made against you and mention was made of disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, among other things, yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, were you suspended from your post in late August 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a short answer to this question. I would have to clarify something in a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never handed an official document saying that I'm being suspended nor did I ever receive a decision on disciplinary action against me. I think I was in the field, perhaps this had to do with the preparations for the trip to Foca, and the then assistant minister for police Mr. Kovac came to Bijeljina, held a working meeting with the employees of the CSB Bijeljina, ministry CSB employees, and without my presence. And after that meeting I met with Mr. Kovac, and I also have witnesses who can confirm that. Now, having heard what -- about what this whole matter was about, I understood that there would follow a decision on my suspension, a decision sent by the ministry. When I met with this man, he was in the company of armed men and he was very, very rude and brusque with me. And I will have to quote now the words he said, and my apologies for it. He addressed me saying the following: You have done your job professionally and you deserve an A for it, an A plus, however, we needed you as a condom for a one-time operation. Now, I hope that based on the words that I've just quoted, and I have witnesses, I believe that it clearly shows what the purpose and what the objective of these men was, Mr. Kovac and some other people around him from the Bijeljina CSB. Before the meeting, Mr. Kovac went to the parking or depot where the vehicles which had been confiscated were kept. There were some 150 vehicles there. He also toured the gym of the Bijeljina CSB which was full of various items that had been stolen in fact, stolen goods, and he inspected that. So I believe that I have answered your question and that they are what you wanted me to say, basically, that you're satisfied with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After this did you leave the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I could be found at home in my house in Bijeljina and if there was a need, they could come and ask me to come and assist them while I spent there a month or so, but no one showed up to talk to me, which would have been the logical course. They should have taken a statement from me because of the allegations and the charges against me, because basically the charge -- the basic charge was that I took this poker machine without authorisation. And the second man from the ministry, as it were, this was something that was done -- that should have been done with his approval, because if I was -- if there were these charges against me and that this was without authorisation, then I should have been asked by him at least why I had done it without his approval. And a month later --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, sir. I know that this part of your testimony is a bit sensitive and emotional for you, but please try to speak slowly because what we have in the transcript is quite the opposite of what you said. You said that they were supposed to take a statement from you, or, rather, you said: They were supposed to take a statement from me because my greatest error was that I had taken a poker machine. And here it reads without the approval of the second man from the ministry. That should read: That should have been done with his approval and I should have been questioned about this, why I did that without his approval. However, I understood your answer to be something quite different. So could you please repeat. Did you have authorisation from Mr. Cedo Kljajic, the undersecretary for public security of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you something. I'm not emotional at all. As far as I'm concerned, when that issue is at question at this point in time I'm totally cool. I couldn't do anything of that sort without asking my superior. At that point in time, my superior was Cedo Kljajic, and I did ask him. I told him about this problem, if I can call it a problem, and I already mentioned yesterday that this poker machine - and that was a small machine, it was about the size of this screen - that we should give it to the man who was supposed to be our insider at a certain point in time. We needed him so that we could learn from him what was going on in Janja and whether some Serb -- some members of Serb paramilitary units were trying to put pressure on the Janja inhabitants and so on and so forth. So I addressed the undersecretary. I told him what the problem was, and I suggested that it would be a good idea, with his approval, for me to take that poker machine and give it to that person who was of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did he approve that course of action for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And he said, Go there, take that poker machine, and do it that way. However, I did not really want to take the poker machine without leaving any kind of paper trail. However, the man who issued that poker machine to me, he did make an Official Note in handwriting and he said -- which read, By approval, by authorisation of the undersecretary Cedo Kljajic, the poker machine is being issued to the following person. He signed that he had handed it over, and I signed to show that I had received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So after a month that no one came to take a statement from you, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an ugly thing happened first, and the ugliness is in the following: The local authorities headed by Mr. Vajo [phoen] Mandic brought a summons or call-up papers. They -- I was supposed to report to a military post, and they -- and to report as a soldier, not as a reserve officer, to report there so that I could be sent to Majevica, to the front line. Now, if you allow me, I would like to provide some explanation here. That month, without any kind of protection, I was exposed to all manner of provocation and I was even physically assaulted in Bijeljina. The only thing I thought at that time was that I should leave everything behind me; that I should take my family, get on a bus, and head towards Serbia, probably Belgrade, and then from there go on abroad. But, frankly speaking now as I sit here, I think I was afraid. I was afraid of the fact that I had participated directly in the arrest of Vujo Vuckovic, Zuco, that I opposed the paramilitary units in Bijeljina, that I stood up to them, and most of them actually came from Serbia. The second fear that I had was that if I headed with my family for Belgrade, that someone at the border crossing - well, there weren't really border crossings but there was a check-point - so that one of the local policeman would stop me, take me off the bus, arrest me, and then I wouldn't know what would happen to my family. So that I was forced, actually, to stay in Bijeljina. Now, when this snide call-up or summons came from Bojan Andric, I tried to actually disregard it. And in a couple of days I didn't respond in any way. And then Predrag Salapura from the Main Staff of the VRS came to me and he offered that I join the ranks of the VRS, which at that time to me looked like a very attractive proposal. I told Mr. Salapura the problem that I had with my family, and they promised that they would protect my family, that there wouldn't be any pressure put on them. However, unfortunately when I left, my wife and my two children accompanied by 15 specials from the Serbian MUP were moved out from the Muslim house in Bijeljina and then I was provided sleeping quarters by some friends in Belgrade and that's how it transpired. And I'm under oath here and I vouch to you that every word I said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if there are no objections, I would move to have the MFI removed from this document, as this witness actually recognised this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. We can de-MFI it for the reason that the witness, indeed, has recognised the report, but I'm just making the observation that nothing of what the witness has said so far actually relates to this document. I mean, the poker machine isn't mentioned, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. On page 4 of the document is -- the poker machine is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. I accept that. It's just that we can only see the page that is on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the MFI qualification is removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, after you joined the ranks of the VRS, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andan, in the fall of 1992, did you see Vitomir Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I began to work in intelligence of the VRS, in an intelligence department, and my task was to go to Pale. And then, on my own initiative, I went to Lukavica because I heard that Vitomir Popovic -- Vitomir Zepinic, my apologies, was in Lukavica, that he was a VRS officer there, and I wanted to meet him, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say that he was a VRS officer. What type of duty was he on and who was his superior officer, if you know? I mean, what was the situation when you went to Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in the security department, and his immediate superior was Colonel Marko Lugonja, and I think, or, rather, I'm certain, that at the time had the rank and he bore the insignia of captain of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that his family was in Nis, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, too. And I even believe that he told me that he had already visited them once, and he said he was very grateful to his immediate superior Lugonja who allowed him to use his own vehicle, his vehicle, to go and see his family in Nis. He told me this his family was indigent there, that they had very meager means and poor living quarters, and he had to go there to try and help them improve their living quarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened after that to Mr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. After he left, I read an information. Mr. Zepinic went on a furlough. Every 40 days, officers were allowed ten days of furlough. So he received an official car, he went on furlough, he went to Nis to get his family. They all boarded that official car. The car was found some place near Subotica, close to the Hungarian border. It was found by the Serbian police. Since the registration plates belonged to the VRS, they notified the Main Staff or maybe somebody else, I'm not quite sure exactly, but I know that Mr. Lugonja sent some men to get the car back. Later on, it transpired that he had crossed the state border and left the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Andan, do you know that the government headed by Prime Minister Djeric collapsed, if I may put it that way, or resigned, to put it in another way, and do you maybe know when that happened? I know that you are not very good with dates, but do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 1992. I do not know the exact date. Of course, many problems had accumulated. I consider Mr. Djeric to be an honest man, and at that point in time he was simply unable to deal with the crime that had accumulated in the Serbian ranks. He probably wasn't courageous enough and he couldn't deal with that so he resigned, and I think that led to the resignation of the whole government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1994 Mico Stanisic was appointed once again to the post of the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting with Mico Stanisic and what was the topic of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we place that in time. I assume you're talking about in 1994 after Mico was appointed again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness can give the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure how long it was after he was appointed, but sometime towards the end of 1993 in the Sarajevo settlement of Grbavica I established an intelligence point. That's where I performed my duties. All of a sudden I received a call from Mr. Dragan Kitso [phoen]; he was head of national security at the time. He asked me whether I could come and meet him and Mr. Stanisic in the Kikinda facility. That's one or two kilometres away from Pale towards Jahorina. I accepted that invitation the same day or the day after, and I met with Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kitso in an office. After a bit of a small talk, we began with the official part of the meeting. And that's when Mr. Stanisic offered me the following: He told me that he wanted to speak to me about the establishment of a unit. I'm not sure whether that unit was supposed to be part of the state security or public security, but here I would opt for the state or national security. He told me that this unit was supposed to deal with war criminals. The time had come for everybody who committed war crimes to be investigated and prosecuted. The time had come for the final show-down with all those people who were engaged in criminal activities. And I assume that Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Kijac, and their associates thought about this problem and decided to speak to me first, to ask me whether I would be willing to accept this duty, whether I would be willing to begin a war of a different kind, so to speak. I was also told that if I accept this, that within a few days I would be given 150.000 German marks in order to equip the unit with all the necessary equipment. I was told that the funds had already been allocated for that. I was surprised by the invitation and by the conversation. I told Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kijac that I needed some time to think it over, but I also told them that I had one precondition for all this, and that was that I was supposed to choose the personnel. Mr. Stanisic immediately accepted that. I told them that I would need two squads within the unit, one squad to gather intelligence and the other squad to analyse intelligence. So I wanted to have two squads, operative and analytical. I think that there was also a preliminary discussion about the premises in Pale where this was supposed to be situated. I asked Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Kijac that there should be no influence of political structures of Republika Srpska over me, and they promised me that. So that's how this conversation ended. And I was supposed to contact them again after some time, three days, four days, seven days, and we were supposed to arrange my transfer from the military to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not. I will try to explain this. I didn't know at the time but later on I heard that Mr. Stanisic and part of his team, I don't know what team that was, had already began working on these issues. He had already began to collect certain intelligence related to organised crime. I heard that some high-ranking persons and their brothers were involved in it. I heard that politics interfered again, and nothing came out of this unit. Also, nothing came out of Mico Stanisic being appointed again to the post of the minister. When they learned that he began gathering this intelligence, he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is all [Previous translation continues] ... I said that -- I see that the record doesn't record what I said. I finished my direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. My name's Tom Hannis, I'm the Prosecutor in this case, or one of the Prosecutors in this case. I want to start by going back to the first day you were on direct examination and you were talking a little bit about your background in the MUP. At page 21343 you told us you were holding the position of senior inspector 1st class. I had a question for you: How many senior inspectors 1st class were there in the BiH SUP at that time? Was there only one or were there several of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only one, several.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that on the public security or the state security side of the house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the public security side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Early on you told us that you considered yourself an operative by nature. Can you tell us your definition of an operative. What was an operative or what did you do as an operative?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Are you referring to my operative work in the state security service? Because while I was in the public security service I was more of a manager and less of an operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. For the moment let's talk specifically about in state security.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the state security service. I was an operative in the emigration department. More specifically, I was in charge of gathering the intelligence about the Ustasha emigration in the area of West Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from when till when did you hold that position and do that work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to know about my whole work in the state security service, I can tell you that I began working there in March 1976. I worked in the surveillance service first. And if you're not quite familiar, maybe you will not receive an interpretation that will be clear to you immediately. I spent a period of time as part of the surveillance team that followed the persons of interest to the service. I would also be engaged during that time with the technical part of the job, that is, installation of the equipment and eavesdropping of the persons of the interest to the service. The third phase of my work was in the operative department for emigration. I worked there until approximately the end of 1983. That's when I was transferred to the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what work were you doing in 1991 and 1992 before the split of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you that I was a senior inspector 1st class in the police administration in the public security service of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And briefly, those duties included going out into the field and doing inspections; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a primary task, to control the police stations. I told you that we had various regions and we had to visit every police station at least once a year. We had to perform the supervisory inspection, we had to write the report related to that inspection, and specify measures that that police station was supposed to undertake within a certain dead-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If, for example, you saw problems in a CSB or an SJB, did you personally have the authority to compel or impose corrective actions, or could you only report it up and it was for someone else to direct that action be taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, first I had to observe the problem, then I had to report my -- to my superiors about that problem in writing. In that memo or record, it was part of my duties to also propose to my superior the measures that had to be undertaken in order to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did that work? Did you also give a copy -- of your proposals that went up to your superior, did you also give a copy of those to the SJB chief or the person inspected? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning we did not have the duty to forward a copy of that to the chief of the police station or chief of the centre, but then there was an instructive dispatch that introduced the obligation that the person who was inspected had to sign that he or she was in agreement with the supervisory inspection. One copy was then left with the chief of the centre or station, and the other copy I took to Sarajevo and handed over to my superior. However, after this instructive dispatch, we had to write our report on the spot, because we had to leave a copy in the hands of the chief who had been inspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the practice in terms of what the superior did with your recommendations? Were you informed about whether or not your recommendations were accepted or whether they were rejected or modified? What was the process in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: When the supervisory inspection was completed, we were supposed to meet with a particular officer and inform him about our findings. If there was something urgent, then my superior would order me or the inspector who did the job to write a dispatch, an urgent memo. The dispatch would be signed by the chief, and it would contain the immediate measures that had to be undertaken. Later on, in the second phase, after there was a chance to have a discussion about the whole of the report, we would write a separate report containing only the necessary measures. It would go something like: This was observed, has to be resolved until this dead-line; that was observed, has to be resolved until this dead-line. So that was the usual procedure, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Andan, you, I think, told us that you had been interviewed by personnel from the Office of the Prosecutor on two occasions, I think once in Brcko and once in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember me being one of the persons who interviewed you in Brcko, the one you described as the more friendly, less formal interview?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I don't remember. But if -- I'm quite glad that I put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, me too. Do you remember the investigator from New Zealand who participated in that discussion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Until I see him, I'm unable to remember. I remember one investigator, and that's the one who spoke to me in Banja Luka. And if you want me to say something about that, I can tell you something about that particular investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's all right. I want to return to the inspection process just for a minute. Typically if you went out to an SJB to do an inspection, was there a standard procedure or protocol you follow in terms of who you talk to, what kinds of documents or log-books you looked at? Was there some kind of routine that you followed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us what that involved.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were two kinds of inspections, announced and unannounced. An announced inspection would be performed only after the relevant organ would be notified in advance that on a certain date two inspectors - it was usually two inspectors - would come in order to inspect the particular police administration or police station. Unannounced supervisory inspection would be performed when the crime service or the police administration service would receive information about some problems in the work of a police station. That's when we would usually receive an oral order to find all relevant facts. So there was regular supervisory inspection; that was announced. And there was also the other kind. When we would arrive to the police station, we would immediately contact the commander of the police station. Later on when there were security centres, we had to visit the chief of the centre and notify him that we were going to perform a supervisory inspection of this particular or that particular police station. After we did that, we would have to return to him and inform him about our findings. After we spoke to a commander, we would ask him to give us all the documents in the particular police station; daily event log-book, other registers, KU register, and all other log-books and registers stipulated by the internal regulations and by the Law on the Interior of the Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina. Once this part was finished, because the police and the crime service shared some of the tasks, we insisted, particularly during the last ten years, that the police had to take a more prominent role in resolving the crimes in their relevant areas. So the police would receive every notification about every crime committed. During our inspection we would also contact chief of the crime service in order to find out what percentage of crimes were resolved. And in the end we would also determine the level of order and discipline in the police station. At the end of the supervisory inspection, there would be a working meeting with all the authorised officials belonging to a certain police station. We would briefly inform them about the situation as we had found it, and we would give them brief instructions related to their future work. So that was more or less what we did. I hope that I gave you an appropriate answer. It would usually take two working days, two times eight hours, and then that would be the end of our supervisory inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell me where in the rules we might find this description of the procedure for carrying out an inspection like this? Would that be in the Rules on Internal Organisation of the MUP, or is it in some other rule book that I don't know about? Do you know? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was more of an internal document or regulation that we used in the police administration. It was available to us, and that regulation lists all points based on which this inspection or audit was to be conducted. I don't believe that the public security service also applied that because the nature of their job was different. And it wasn't provided for by the Law on Internal Affairs either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I know you're talking from your experience when you were working as an inspector in public security before the split. Was the same procedure applied in the RS MUP after April 1992 in terms of how inspections were supposed to be conducted, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that in 2000 when I returned to the MUP of the RS, my first inspection or audit was the one I conducted in Visegrad, and I applied all methods that I applied before the war. So I did about it the same way, because nothing had changed in essence. Possibly the legal procedure had changed somewhat. The greatest change was that it was no longer the socialist republic, but we did the same policing jobs after the war as before the war and during the war, too, whenever an audit was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I want to talk a little bit about the -- your testimony beginning at page 21372 last week on Thursday. Mr. Zecevic was talking to you about the personnel policy in the BiH MUP under Mr. Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could show the witness Exhibit 1D347.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, this was a document you were shown before. It will be up on the screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think I need to go to paragraph 6 which I think is on page 2. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You recall seeing this? This is a document from Mr. Cengic in the SDA. Do you remember seeing this before, last week?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you see the last sentence in paragraph 6 says: "We need to persevere until the end with these changes in the SJB and achieving ethnic balance." Now, to me, when that says achieving ethnic balance, it sounds like, at least in his view, that there was some sort of pre-existing imbalance in the SJB or the SUP. Do you know, in late 1991, what the relative percentages of Croats, Muslims, and Serbs were in the police? Do you have any idea about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state any percentages, but I think that the Muslims were the most numerous, followed by the Serbs, and the Croats were third because they were the least numerous in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about in the JNA; do you know the relative percentages among the three primary ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Serbs were in first place, followed by the Muslims, Croats, and finally, Slovenians. Well, I skipped the Macedonians; there were some, I'm sorry. And the Montenegrins were actually quite strongly represented in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that you noticed that the personnel policy that was being pursued was, in your words, an unprincipled one, and you gave us a couple of examples of what appeared to be bad choices. You told us about Mr. Jasarevic who was promoted from a sort of an assistant position, I think, in the SJB all the way up to head of a task for defence preparations. But I want to ask you, would you agree with me that at this time in late 1991 and early 1992 that all three of the national political parties, the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS, were trying their best to manipulate the appointments in the police at all levels, at the republic level, at the regional level, and the local? Would you agree with that as a general principle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say that I heard you say "Pasarevic," whereas the name is actually "Jasarevic," or maybe I misheard the interpretation. But I do ask you to be a bit more specific. When you say manipulate, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I mean that they were more interested in getting someone appointed based on that individual's political affiliation, that is, it was more important to get somebody who was in the SDS, for example, or friendly to the SDS, rather than someone who was a professional policeman or qualified based on their experience. Same goes for HDZ and SDA.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such examples in abundance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me ask you, because I don't know if I've heard before, before -- well, I guess it didn't come up before, right, because before the national parties came into existence, there was just one party and that was the communist party, and everybody in the police sort of had to be a member of the communist party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that time appointments, I take it, were made more on merit rather than politics; somebody got appointed head of the SJB because they had experience as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must say that even then the ethnic composition of the personnel was considered, at least in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It couldn't happen that the chief of the -- of an SJB was a Serb, that the commander was a Serb, and that the head of another organisational unit was also a Serb. Let me give an example. When I was appointed commander at -- in Novo Sarajevo, the chief of the police station was a Croat, his assistant Kemal Sabovic was a Muslim, and the second assistant was Vitomir Zepinic. I was commander of the police station, whereas the chief of the crime enforcement service was a Muslim. Along with all the references that you needed at the time, and I mean first and foremost the results of your work, what was considered also was the ethnic composition and the position to be taken by a member of -- or, rather, by a person of a certain ethnic affiliation, and of course you had to be a member of the communist party, which I was, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about some appointments of Serbs to positions in the SUP before the war broke out in April 1992, and maybe a few shortly thereafter. Borislav Maksimovic was, I think, SJB chief in Vogosca, and it's my information that before that, before he came to the police, he had been a journalist. Did you know about that? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Milenko Tepavcevic was in that position. Maybe immediately before the war he was replaced by somebody else. But I do not remember that this somebody was this man Maksimovic you have mentioned. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Risto Perisic, chief in Visegrad who had been a school teacher before being appointed to that post; did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't interested in that at the time. I covered Eastern Herzegovina. I heard of Mr. Perisic a bit later, but I didn't know that -- of this personnel change. I think that Mr. Stambolic covered the area of Eastern Bosnia and he was certainly better informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more and then I'll move on. How about a Radomir Bjelanovic, chief in Vlasenica until the latter half of May 1992. Prior to his appointment he'd worked at the bauxite mine in Milici and didn't have any prior police experience. Did you know him? He later was then, I think, chief in Milici after May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to meet him during the war. He wasn't in that position long because he clashed with the director of the bauxite mine. I know that he didn't work in the police force before the war and that he was -- he joined the police during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the director of the bauxite mine that he clashed with, was that Rajko Dukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Rajko Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The same Rajko Dukic who was president of the SDS Main Board in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same Rajko Dukic who, as far as I know, was in charge of Serbian personnel for a while, I mean the distribution of Serbian personnel. Vitomir Zepinic was also a product of his personnel policy, because he appointed him to his position because they hailed from the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And had Mr. Zepinic had any prior police experience before that appointment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we can say that he did have previous experience. And he was the assistant of the joint forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Kosovo at the time of the demonstrations there. He was assistant commander at the time, and he did have some experience. Not necessarily enough to be appointed to that position, in my modest opinion, but he did have some police experience, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to the beginning of March 1992. You are well familiar with the event, I think, in the 1st of March when a Serb wedding guest was shot, and then shortly thereafter barricades were set up all around the town. You know the event I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have already discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And when you were talking with Mr. Zecevic, you talked about, I think, you and other members of the police were called in to the building and sort of stood around for a long time with nothing to do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know which building you're referring to. Please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understood from Mr. Zecevic's question at page 21384 that it was in the MUP building of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that not correct? Is that the building where you were all gathered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you don't remember seeing Mr. Stanisic in that building that night, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had seen Mr. Kljajic. I'm not sure that I saw Mr. Stanisic. I cannot confirm that or deny that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Momo Mandic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see him during the night, but during the day he came to his office. I have already said as much. And then my friend Kemal Sabovic went to those barricades with him. That's when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness 65 ter 822D1. I don't know if that received an exhibit number or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I'll show you a document that you were shown by Mr. Zecevic when discussing this event. And it's a document that has a typed block at the end as the "Serb Crisis Staff." Now, when was the first time you saw this document? Did you see it in 1992 or did you only see it when you came to testify? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 I didn't have the chance to see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you -- [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. Do you know who was a member or a part of this Crisis Staff for the Serbian People of BiH in March 1992? Do you know any the people who might have been on that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the composition of the Crisis Staff, but I heard at the time that the chief of the Crisis Staff was Rajko Dukic and that Mr. Mandic had direct communication with him. I do not know who the other members were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This document is headed as "Conditions for Negotiating," and there are certain demands made. Do you know to whom this document was sent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about do you know if anybody in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH investigated this document and this incident concerning the barricades?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the state security service rather than the public security service conducted investigation, not triggered by this report but due to the barricades. The state security service did conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know it's a couple of minutes early, but this would be a convenient point for me to break and check something before I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, before we leave this document, I just want to draw your attention to two or three items and ask you to keep them in mind when I move on to the next area. Among these, what I would describe as demands from the Crisis Staff of the Serbian People in BiH, number one talks about "all further activities in the campaign about trying to declare a sovereign and independent Bosnia." Number 6 talks about a demand that the TV and radio be urgently divided. And number 8 - we need to go to the next page in English - but you can see your number 8 talks about the resignation of the Crisis Staff and Mr. Ganic resigning from his post. Do you know who Mr. Ganic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I must point out that there's a problem with the air condition again. When I first sat down here this morning, there wasn't so much draft. Could this be taken care of somehow? Because it was much more pleasant when I first came here this morning. Or maybe if I could get a cap or hat. Yes, I know who Ganic was. No need, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, we've historically had some climate problems in this courtroom, and I would join in your request. We'll see what we can do about that. But tell us, who was Mr. Ganic? What was his full name and who was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ejub Ganic after the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina was elected to the position of a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Yugoslav. I believe, or, rather, I hope I stated this accurately. He was appointed as a Yugoslav anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I think you told me earlier that you understood that the state security service you believe carried out some sort of investigation of how the barricades came about and who was involved. I'd like to show you a document now that is Exhibit P911. 911.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a hard copy in the B/C/S, if the usher could hand that to you. I think it will speed things up because it's several pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it would be very helpful if you could give the tab number, as well, of the documents. And the binder you're citing from, it is your binder or Defence binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry, Your Honour. P911 is at tab 11 of the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Take your time to look through that, Mr. Andan. And when you're ready to, let me know by telling me whether or not you've seen this document before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, I didn't think to give it to him before he went out on the break. I'll try to do that the next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan. I take it, by your careful read of that document, you had not seen it before today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see, it's described as a security information in relation to the events of 1, 2, 3, and 4 of March in Sarajevo. Given that you were present in Sarajevo at the time of these events, and having read it, can you tell us, based on the parts in the report that describe events that you may have personal knowledge of, is it consistent with what you saw and heard at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about things that I haven't had personal involvement in, but there were two events when we were called up to come to the MUP and we learned that night that the Serbs were setting up barricades, that they wanted to separate Sarajevo or divide it into two parts. And the second event was when I went with Mr. Music, my colleague, to his house, where I saw a lot of armed men, but at that point in time and not even later, I have to say, did I realise that they were actually erecting barricades. I did see armed men. They were leaving their homes with long-barrelled weapons. But at that point in time I wasn't aware that they were setting up barricades. So I can confirm that basically the intelligence that is set out here, and based on my experience with those two events, incidents that I mentioned, I can confirm that this is probably correct. Now, I didn't have any information about Ilidza or Ilijas or Vares or any of the other places that are mentioned in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another document related to this event. This is P643. This is a shorter document. And I'd like to hand you a hard copy of this one as well. It's tab number 12 in the Prosecution's list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, this is -- well, the cover letter is dated the 13th of March, 1992, to the minister of the Internal Affairs from the subsecretary in charge of SDB. Before you look at the contents, can I ask you, do you know who the subsecretary in charge of SDB was at that time? Can you recognise the name or signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Branko Kvesic. He was the undersecretary for state security and he was of Croat ethnicity. I don't know if this is actually his signature, but I do know that he was the undersecretary for the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could, could you just take a quick look at it, not necessarily reading the entire thing at the moment, to tell me whether or not you've seen it before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll see on the second page it is a list of MUP employees who took part in the activities related to the barricades in early March. I see number 1 is Momcilo Mandic. Were you aware that Mr. Mandic had taken part in those events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you know about his participation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that night, as we were sitting in our offices, one of our colleagues mentioned that Momo had organised those barricades, but I have to say, he didn't even try to hide his activities. He wasn't going to hide it. He was one of the leaders on those barricades, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On your page 4, and it's English page 3, number 13 is listed as Malko Koroman. Did you have any knowledge or information about his participation in the barricades?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, obviously this -- there is an error in the translation; it's not "Malko" Koroman but "Marko" Koroman. But I don't know anything about his activities during the barricade events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And if you could go to the last page. And there's a paragraph that says: "In the Crisis Staff of the SDS, among others, the following persons were engaged: Mr. Mandic; 2. Mico Stanisic; 3. Dragan Kijac; 4. Dragan Devedlaka; and 5. Cedo Kljajic." Were you aware about the participation of those last four in the events involving the barricades in early March 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say again, I did see Cedo Kljajic that night on the premises of the Ministry of the Interior. It is possible that he went and met with these other men at some point during the night, but for Cedo I can claim here with certainty that he was not a member of the staff. For Momcilo Mandic, I know that he was there. But about the other men, the Kijac and Devedlaka, I don't know anything about that. As for Cedo Kljajic, I was there that night in the office, and I did see him there. I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I take it from your answer you didn't see him there all night, you saw him there for some shorter period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw him on several occasions actually, and I believe that even in the morning when we brought this fresh bread, still warm, from Bascarsija that he was with us there. He partook in our breakfast. Later on, I went -- well, you know, it is possible that someone might even say that they saw me on the barricades, because at one point in time I went home during that night, but I actually did not go there. So as I said, Mandic didn't -- was there; he didn't even hide that fact. But as for Cedo and Devedlaka and Kijac, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, could you speak slower because a number of the things that -- words was not recorded. In 32/25, the witness -- the witness, I think, said something different than it is -- it is recorded. "He partook in our breakfast. Later on, I went -- well, you know, it is possible that someone might" - might have seen me, I believe - "that they saw me on the barricades, because at one point in time I went home during that night, but I actually didn't go there." I believe the witness gave a quite different answer, I mean, with a different meaning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would prefer that there's an opportunity that this be dealt with when the transcript is listened to and before its finalised. Otherwise, I would request my learned friend to make a note and it's something he can address in re-direct, if it hasn't been taken care of after the audio has been listened to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Hannis, if it is something which significantly changes the meaning of what the witness intended to convey, it should be dealt with as early as possible. I would suggest that the witness be referred to what is recorded, and if you could phrase the question again. And, Mr. Andan, one of the difficulties that -- one of the problems that should be avoided is you're speaking so quickly that the interpreters are unable to accurately interpret what you're saying so as to convey what you intend to tell us. So, Mr. Hannis, if you could ask the question again and invite the witness to repeat that account.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was - and, Mr. Andan, you've heard the discussion. Let me ask you again, and please try and recall your answer and tell it to us again but slowly so the interpreters can follow. My question was: "I take it from your answer you didn't see him," meaning Cedo Kljajic, "there all night, you saw him there for some shorter period of time; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what was said. I said that when we received this call, when the phone call came telling us to come to the offices of the republican Ministry of the Interior, I found Mr. Cedo Kljajic in his office then. A little later, sometime in the morning hours when Mr. Teufik Music and I went to Bascarsija, and as I said we also went by Vratnik from where we brought warm flatbread and somuns, we found Cedo Kljajic in the office and he ate those somuns with us, together. I little later that morning, I said that I went to the barricade, and I described that a little earlier, and based on that one could claim that I, too, had participated in organising the setting up of those barricades, which I did not. You can see that there's -- from the Official Notes there's nothing that would put me in connection with setting up the barricades. But as for Cedo Kljajic, I did say that I saw him in the morning hours in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess what I was trying to establish was, were there periods of time during that night when you did not see Mr. Kljajic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such periods. We were mobilised in the evening, sometime around midnight. We spent the whole time on the same floor. We were not all the time with him. But I mentioned two moments when I saw him, the first time when we greeted him and when we asked him what was going on and why we had been called up. He didn't have any specific answer to that. And then the second time that I saw him was when we returned from Bascarsija with the somuns. Whether he left his office, whether he met anybody, I cannot speak about that. But I did see him on those two occasions during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I next want to show you Exhibit P1110, which is at tab 6 of the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I can hand you a hard copy of this as well. I will tell you, this is a document that's in evidence already in this case. It's an intercepted telephone conversation that is listed as having occurred on the 2nd of March, 1992, between Jovo Jovanovic, Radovan Karadzic, and Radovan Karadzic and Mico Stanisic. While you're looking through that, let me ask you, Do you know who Jovo Jovanovic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Jovo Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You will see in the conversation Mr. Jovanovic is talking to Mr. Karadzic and at one point in time, I'm not sure which page it is in the B/C/S, but Mr. Jovanovic says: "We want to remove barricades. We reached an agreement and that's all. Rajko just passed the information." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's on your page 2.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it appears to be a discussion about the barricades. If you could go on, about the middle of that page, and Mr. Jovanovic says: "Just what we wanted, there won't be any negotiations with Europe about either sovereign or non-sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina until the parties agree on that one." You remember that Crisis Staff of the Serbian People document we looked at earlier and the demands. Do you recall that was one of the demands? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I remember right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just a few lines down below that you see Jovanovic reports: "They agreed to dismiss Ganic's staff." Do you remember that was number 8 in the Crisis Staff document list of demands, was having Ganic resign or be removed? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if we could go to page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you I think it begins at the bottom of page 4. You see Mico Stanisic is coming on to the phone and speaking with Mr. Karadzic. And I think on your page 5 you're seeing they're talking about removing the barricades. You see that? And there's a mention of Pofalici. Do you know where that was and whether there was a barricade in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- oh, I found it. Yes, I know where Pofalicis are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall if there was a barricade in that area on the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to have you take a look at another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P910, Your Honours. That's at tab 8. It's a short one, but I can hand the witness a hard copy of that with the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, this is another one from the 2nd of March. This is an intercepted telephone conversation between Mico Stanisic and Rajko Dukic. Regarding the Serb Crisis Staff and the barricades, did you know or did you ever hear or learn any information about where they were physically located at that time? Do you know where they were set up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't hear your question. There was an interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you know, did you have any information at the time or subsequently, did you learn about where the Serb Crisis Staff was set up on the 2nd of March during the barricades event?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you had a look at this brief conversation between Mr. Stanisic and Rajko Dukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read all of it. I'll try to read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just let me know when you're done. On your page 1, page 2 of the English, Mr. Dukic is saying: "I just talked with Cengic, and Biljana talked with Alija Izetbegovic." In this context, would you agree with me that Cengic must mean Hasan Cengic from the SDA? I think it's on your page 1 near the bottom.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it's Hasan Cengic because he was in the power then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Biljana in this context would mean, I assume, Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the general -- the rest of the general discussion is Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Dukic congratulating themselves on the success of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my understanding. Not congratulating. What I can see is that that's a conversation Stanisic is having, a professional conversation with Dukic in order to analyse the whole situation and avoid possible future omissions related to barricades. And I think that Dukic said that a big thing had been achieved. I wouldn't understand that as a congratulation; I would, rather, say what I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, English page 3 and your B/C/S page 2, Mr. Stanisic says that he had visited all the check-points, Mr. Dukic said "yes," and then Mr. Stanisic said "Sarajevo is ours." Isn't that some sort of congratulations or report of an achievement? He goes on to say "a hundred per cent." And Mr. Dukic says "we've done a big thing." You don't agree with my interpretation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's simply a declaration of facts. They said that a big thing had been done, and that's a fact. You can interpret that as a congratulation, as a success, but that was simply a fact at that particular point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. One more -- or, I'm sorry, two more, and then we'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could show the witness P1112. This is tab 9 of the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I have another hard copy for you of this one. Again, it's a conversation on the 2nd of March. And the participants in this one are Mico Stanisic and Miroslav Toholj.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read first and then comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Before you do, can I ask you, Do you know who Mr. Toholj was and what his job was at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think he was member of the government, probably minister for religious communities, I think, in the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have any involvement with information or media?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, religious communities and information, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead and have a quick read of that before I ask you any more questions. Thank you. Would you agree that Mr. Toholj seems to be calling Mr. Stanisic to get some information about what's happening because he's wanting to be able to tell about that, to report that to the people? You see in your bottom of your page 1 - English, middle of page 2 - he says: "Well, tell me the general idea so I can tell the people ..."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Going on --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that part. And I see that Mr. Stanisic tells him to go to Rajko Dukic, who is the chief of the Crisis Staff, in order to obtain answers. Stanisic is either avoiding to give him the answers or maybe he didn't know the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, if you could go to the top of your page 2 - again, English, middle of page 2 - Mr. Toholj said: "What are our standpoints?" And Mico Stanisic says -- according to my English translation, he says: "Well, they should be advised to address the Crisis Staff here and Rajko." Now, to me that sounds like Mico Stanisic is at this point in time at the Crisis Staff. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't agree entirely with you. Maybe the Crisis Staff was located close to the location where Mr. Stanisic was. They say "the Crisis Staff here"; maybe the premises were close or maybe in the same town. I have no idea where they were. And Rajko's name is mentioned explicitly here. From this I cannot conclude that Mr. Stanisic is a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wasn't suggesting that. I was just suggesting that his physical presence at that moment was at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to object. First all, the witness was not a party to any of these conversations. Mr. Hannis is reading the intercepts to him and asking him to draw the conclusions which I think amounts to speculations simply, nothing else than that, because the documents talk for themselves. And perhaps, perhaps the Office of the Prosecutor -- in my opinion, the Office of the Prosecutor should have brought the witnesses who were party to the conversation to explain what they meant and what was the gist of the conversation, and not to ask the witness to speculate what the other parties - who were not talking to him, he wasn't present - wanted to say and were thinking about while they were talking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I had -- I was going to intervene earlier in terms of these transcripts, and the -- because I wondered for a moment why it was that whatever your interpretation, whatever inferences you were drawing from the transcript, whereas that's one thing, and you were inviting the witness to accept, or not, your own views as to what it meant. This is similar to the intervention Mr. Zecevic has just made. But I refrained from doing that because I thought that perhaps you were trying to elicit from the witness a sense of what the transcripts meant with a view to asking another question. But if, in fact, that is not your ultimate intention, in other words, if this is not an intermediary stage or preliminary stage to something else you're about to ask, it seems that Mr. Zecevic has a point. Why pursue the angle of what this witness, who happens to be on the stand, makes of these transcripts? He wasn't a party to it. He has a -- if it's left at that, it's a matter of inference and argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I understand what you're saying, Your Honour. I am asking these questions regarding the intercepts and the two documents prior to that, the reports about the events, to lead up to ask a question related to an answer that the witness gave on direct examination at page 21385 when he was asked if he had any information or any intelligence. He said "at the time" -- this is Mr. Zecevic: "At the time did you and [sic] the police administration have any intelligence that Mico Stanisic had any role whatsoever in the barricades on the 2nd of March, 1992, in Sarajevo?" "I did not have any such information." Now, I'm trying to show him that there was information that the security service had and relate this to some other aspects of this witness's situation in the MUP at that time and subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I said, as I thought you might have been aiming at, but it would be -- if you could bring it together more rapidly, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the proper question should have been that Mr. Hannis establishes that, in fact, the security services had that information. We don't know when these intercepts were made. We don't know. We just believe that they were made on the 2nd of March. That is why -- that's the point, you see, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I also intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's up to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply professional intervention. The transcripts of these conversations here, I assume, or, rather, I'm sure that those transcripts originate from the state security service. We in the public security service did not receive any information whatsoever from the state security. This situation related to the barricades. It is possible that my superiors had this information, but this information did not go anywhere below. So if you take the information drafted by the state security service and if you take a look at the addressees, you will see that not even the undersecretary of the public security or the chief of the police administration will be found on the list of addressees. Maybe if somebody sent it down, maybe. But normally we never had that information. Normally in our service every single person who reads a particular information is duty-bound to sign or initial the information signifying that he had read it. We don't have anything like that here. So we don't know whether these transcripts were sent to the minister or other government structures in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I apologise for this intervention. I hope that it was not in vein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andan. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. Mr. Andan, could you please remove your headphones. Thank you. Now, I'm really brought to the point of confusion by this series of interventions. I thought, and please correct me if I'm wrong, but the picture that I had was that in the document P643, which was the 13th March report, that report seemed to include the information at the end that the following members of the Crisis Staff had taken part in the erection of the barricades, and among these members was Mico Stanisic. The subsequent documents that we saw were the transcripts of the intercepts, and there, as far as I could pick it up, but I'm not sure about it because they went very fast, in one conversation Mico Stanisic seemed to -- seemed to accept that the barricades had been established and had no intention of taking them down. In another intercept, the one with Karadzic, I thought that Stanisic said the opposite; namely, that he agreed with Karadzic that these barricades should be removed immediately. So this is where the confusion comes in. And in any case, the witness declared right from the beginning that he had no information about Stanisic's involvement. So I don't know where we're going with all of this, but I would like some clarification, if that is possible, from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, the first thing you said, at page 43, line 10, referring to Exhibit P643, you said the "report seemed to include the information at the end that the following members of the Crisis Staff had taken part in the erection of the barricades, and among these members was Mico Stanisic." And that's not my understanding. 643 is a report -- page 2 of the English says the subject is the list of MUP employees who took part in the activities related to the setting of barricades in the region of Sarajevo in early March 1992. And then on the last page, where Mico Stanisic is listed, it says "in Crisis Staff of SDS, among others, the following persons were engaged," which I take it to mean that Mico Stanisic, an employee of the MUP, was engaged in activities regarding the barricades in the Crisis Staff of the SDS, wherever that was located at the time. And I gather that his involvement is described as contacts and instructions to the people in the field. I think if you read the intercepts, when you have more time to read the whole thing, I think you'll see there's discussion between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Karadzic about talking down the barricades, starting, perhaps, a midnight, because they have gotten some of the concessions that they wanted, and Mr. Ganic resigning, et cetera, et cetera. And in the discussion with Mr. Dukic, he's also discussing taking down the barricades, and they're talking about the need to do that carefully so that their men don't get shot at by the other ethnic parties who have set up their own barricades, et cetera, so it needs to be co-ordinated and done carefully. That's what I read from it, Your Honour, and I don't know if that's answering your question. But all of this was initially brought up to address the suggestion raised by the question on direct exam that Mico Stanisic had nothing to do with the barricades. Now, this witness, I think it's clear, didn't know that about that, didn't have that information, because, as he said, this is a report from state security; he was on the public security side, so he wouldn't have seen it. But I want to establish that there is ample evidence that Mr. Stanisic indeed was involved. And part of what I'm trying to show is that this witness was out of the loop for certain things, which is an important argument to make about the totality of his evidence later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I hear your opinion, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we simply -- Your Honours, we simply do not accept the theory which Mr. Hannis just explained.
