First of all, Your Honours, the question which I posed to the witness was, Had he had the information in the MUP with the operatives, the chief operatives of the public security, did they have the information about any involvement of Mico Stanisic in the barricades. He said that they had information that behind the barricades are Rajko Dukic and Momo Mandic, and that is the all information that they had at that point. And he explained that Momo Mandic was not even hiding that. He came to his office and he took Kemal Sabovic with him and went to through barricades, and then Kemal Sabovic had problems with the Muslim leadership of the MUP because he went with Momo Mandic through the barricades. So what I tried to establish is the public -- the knowledge of this witness. Now Mr. Hannis is trying to speculate, basically, because the witness doesn't have any information. He says, I didn't have the information as a public security. Now he's showing him some alleged information, which I will at the end explain why I say alleged information, from the state security that Mico Stanisic had any involvement in that. And I -- that is why -- that was the gist of my objection. Because this witness cannot help in any case. And it wasn't the direct -- the question which I posed on direct, so it doesn't come from the direct examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think this is as far as we can take it, unless you have some --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I make a reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two points I need to address. One was the suggestion before that I, rather than asking this witness to comment, I needed to call witnesses who know about the conversation or participated in the conversation. One witness I can't call. The other point is: Mr. Zecevic needs to go to the transcript to see what question he asked and see why I'm trying to follow up. Transcript page 21385, line 12: "Q. Mr. Andan, at that time did you and [sic] the police administration have any intelligence that Mico Stanisic had any role whatsoever in the barricades on the 2nd of March ... in Sarajevo?" To me, in English, "did you" could mean "you personally" or "you guys" in police administration. And police administration could mean just generally police administration, or it could mean a specific department. But the way it's phrased, it's not clear. And then, when he said "I did not have any ... information," the next question from

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC IS
utterances.text: "Have you heard from any of your colleagues subsequently that any of them had any such information?" Colleagues in that context could be anybody else in the police, state security, public security, et cetera. That's why I felt I was entitled to go into what I've been going into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. It's time for the break, so let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, I have one more to show you, one more intercept to show you on this topic, but before I do, let me ask you a couple of general questions. Are you familiar with the principle "the need to know" in terms of security work? Do you know what I mean when I use that term?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In my brief job in my army doing some kind of security work, we were instructed to follow the principle of "the need to know," meaning that I was not to share information that I received in trying to collect information, or review intercepted conversations, et cetera. I was not to share that with someone unless they had a need to know; the principle being you don't want to give out sensitive security information to just anybody. Now, maybe you're familiar with that idea under a different name, but I assume that's how you worked in the state security service during your time there. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Once intelligence is received, it must be forwarded to the superior officer in writing and cannot be discussed, not even with colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the reasons or the logic behind that is you want to be able to be certain about controlling that information so that it doesn't get to inappropriate places; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and it musn't be commented publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in the context of these -- the state security report about the incidents surrounding the barricades in early March, it's not unusual that you wouldn't be aware of these intercepted conversations or that report we saw in Exhibit P643 because you were on the public security side and didn't have a reason or a need to know about that; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but sometimes the state security service did release some information downward and we would get acquainted with it. I've already explained as much. And each one of us had to sign to confirm that we were privy to that information. We were duty-bound not to spread that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. But in this case you never received any information about this state security report or these intercepted conversations concerning the barricades events; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. We received no intelligence about that event from the state security service, or, indeed, these intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. With that, I want to show you one last one related to this, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's P981. If the usher could hand you a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Judge Delvoie, it's tab 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see Mr. Aleksic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to my learned friend for complaining before he even asked his question, but I must follow up on the objections put forward by Mr. Zecevic. The previous intercepted conversations had to do with document P643, which referred to the report about barricades in the territory of Sarajevo. The document Mr. Hannis is now about to show and ask questions about is unrelated to Sarajevo and the events surrounding the barricades. The witness did not take part in the conversations, and in his previous answers he said that he had no information about the barricades in Sarajevo. Therefore, in my submission, this document has nothing to do with the witness. Mr. Hannis can read it to him and the witness could possibly only state his opinion, but I do not believe that is appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We may agree with you, Mr. Aleksic, but perhaps we should hear the question first and then take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I did want to indicate to Your Honours, I agree it's not particularly about Sarajevo. But Exhibit P911, which is the first information report I showed the witness, the one dated the 6th of March, 1992, which is sent to the BiH president, the Assembly chairman, the prime minister, et cetera, is a more broad report not focussing specifically on employees of the MUP but about everyone involved. And part of the reason I'm offering this is because it offers some corroboration of that report to the extent that that report talks about barricades being set up or planned in areas outside Sarajevo proper. And with that I'll ask the question and we'll see how far I get.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, have you had a chance to read that intercept?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You want to take a second to read those two pages to yourself, and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is reading the document, I would appreciate if Mr. Hannis would be so kind to give us the reference in the Exhibit P911 where in that document does it talk about Banja Luka or Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. Can we have the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't say Banja Luka. I said outside of Sarajevo. I would refer you to page 2 of the English, it's footnote 3, which says: "A large number of barricades were set up on the territory of Ilijas, Olovo, Soko, Breza, Pale, Trnovo, Vares, and Rogatica."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely why I'm asking you, Mr. Hannis, because it precisely deals with the municipalities around Sarajevo and doesn't deal with any municipalities outside that territory of Sarajevo. All those municipalities that are listed are the municipalities in the immediate vicinity of the Sarajevo. So, therefore, I just made this observation because I don't see that this document relates in any way with the intercept that you are showing to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The introductory paragraph says that "the service learned that the extremists were planning to block the city from both outside and inside." And I think this intercept shows that there were preparations to stand by for a further, wider blockade, if it was decided to be necessary. That's why I'm offering it or trying to show it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, my question relates to something said at the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S, and Mr. Stanisic -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZUPLJANIN SAYS
utterances.text: "All right. For the most part everything is ready on our side."

utterances.speaker: MR. STANISIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZUPLJANIN SAYS
utterances.text: "We are waiting for the sign. If a total blockade is needed or the rest, it will be done."

utterances.speaker: MR. STANISIC
utterances.text: "Agreed." Were you aware or did you hear that there had been preparations for possible extension of the blockade beyond the immediate area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, with all due respect, I must say it's difficult for me to comment on documents in which I play no role. I am a man who does not like to give partial answers. At any rate, I can say that I was in Sarajevo at the time and doing my work and I did have some information concerning the city of Sarajevo, because during that time-period, since March 1992 or ever since new year, we weren't even tasked to do audits elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was difficult for me to give a comment on something in which I did not take part or possibly only was mentioned by somebody. So if you had a particular or specific question, that would be good then -- because then I could provide a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that and I appreciate that. I take it, then, that your answer to my question was that you don't have any information about that, you didn't hear anything about it at the time or from anyone since then about whether or not there were plans for the possibility of extending blockades beyond the immediate area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain. You may not believe me, but that's up to you. I received more information by watching the news at 7.30 than I would get when I came to work in the morning. We were basically isolated from all the events. We wondered why we were coming to work and what we were getting paid for. Let me tell you one thing: I was brought up by my parents in such a way that they instilled a sense of discipline in me, but I -- in spite of that, I quit going to work at my regular time in the morning, I would get up at 10.00 and then leisurely stroll to work, and nobody, no superior officer of mine, ever bothered to ask me why. I and a few colleagues, at least, had the sense that we were something like outcasts. I don't know whether other colleagues who had party ties were in a different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That takes me to the next thing I wanted to ask you about. At page 21395, you were asked by Mr. Zecevic about whether you had continued working in early April after the MUP was divided. And you gave part of what you've just said now. I want to show you Exhibit P353.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is at tab 16 of the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you may have seen this before.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the memo sent by Mr. Mandic about separating. Do you recall when that memo came out? It's date the 31st of March; were you aware of it that day or the next day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must be a mistake in the interpretation. This document wasn't sent by Mr. Memic but by Mr. Mandic. In my earphones the name I heard was "Memic." Whether I was acquainted with the contents of this document on the same day or on the following day, well, I said to you at the outset that I'm not so good when it comes to dates. But I remember this dispatch very well. I was one of those who were against doing things this way. And I can say to this Trial Chamber that I took this dispatch to Sarajevo TV and gave it to news moderator Puljic [phoen], who told me, yes, I know, I've received a copy from the ministry already, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can I ask you, Why did you take it to the television guy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a sort of resistance of mine against this division. I wanted the wider public to learn about these things. I was unwilling to accept the division of the MUP at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my main reason for showing you that document was to help you out with dates, because I know you've told us you have a hard time with dates. If that dispatch came out on the 31st of March, can you -- can you use that date to help you remember when, for example, Bruno Stojic and the Croats left the MUP? Was it before or after that dispatch came out? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I can say what I -- what occurred to me just now, what -- it came back to me how I got this dispatch in the first place. At the traffic police station there was a working meeting at which Slavko Draskovic informed all staff present what the contents of this dispatch. My wife worked there at the time. There was an accounting department where she had a job. And she called me on the phone to tell me about the dispatch. It was then that I asked for the dispatch for my superiors at the MUP. I wanted to read it. I xerox copied it and took it to the television. I would gladly answer a question whether Mr. Stojic left before or after, but I really don't remember. I don't want to say anything wrong, so I can't give you a precise answer. I do know that he left, and I've already described that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You just mentioned Slavko Draskovic there. Could you remind us who he was and what position he held at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as a telex operator and encoder. Cedo Kljajic had graduated from law school, and up until the multi-party elections he had some sort of job, I don't know what exactly, and then he was appointed co-ordinator at the police administration. Or possibly he was even chief of department, which job he did for a while, and later on he moved on to the city secretariat of the interior. I don't know what exactly he did there. Once the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he went to Trebinje where he became chief of national security and stayed in that position till the end of the war. That's the person I have in mind. Maybe you know another man by the name of Slavko Draskovic, but that's the one I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My memory may be letting me down. I thought there was a Slavko Draskovic who did eventually go to Trebinje, as you said, but earlier in 1992 I understood he had some position, I think, as an assistant minister in the RS MUP and then for a short time was moved to the position of advisor to the minister; do you know of such a person, or am I getting my names mixed up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking of the period of the socialist federal -- the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, and I know that he was not in any higher position. I don't know at the time that he was assistant minister or advisor. I don't know anything about that. But I know for a fact that when I had a problem in Trebinje, he was already at that time the chief for national security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, on the -- after Mandic's dispatch on the 31st of March, did you notice whether he or any of the other ethnic Serbs continued to come to work at your building in Sarajevo? Or were you the only one still coming in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was what was confusing for all of us at the ministry [Realtime transcript read in error "military police military"] because Mandic continued coming to the ministry not regularly. Now, Vitomir Zepinic, who was the deputy minister, he came to work regularly. And there were several other employees of Serb ethnicity in my administration, Vojo Gavrilovic and two other colleagues, who came to work as I did. To be honest, you know, I went there 10.00, was there till about 12.00, and then I went back home. So it was totally chaotic. We didn't really have any direction, as it were. There wasn't even a regular command, to put it that way. So there were colleagues who kept on coming to work, but there were others that I didn't see anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the page 55/15. It says "military police military." And it says "police ministry," I believe that was what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Andan? That makes sense. The transcript says you said it was "confusing for all of us in the 'military police military,'" and we're assuming you said "police ministry."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it from your previous answer that some of your Serb colleagues had left after Mr. Mandic's memo or dispatch. Did any of those colleagues who had left get in touch with you and try to encourage you to leave and join them in their newly-created ministry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such attempts. There were some phone calls. One of them was rather unpleasant; it came in the middle of the night when they were checking my ethnicity, what my Slava was, and my background. And in the end they said something to the effect, You're a traitor of your own people, and so on. But there were also honourable discussions and conversations where people were telling me that perhaps I wasn't aware of the whole picture, that as a Serb employee and as a Serb, a Serb person, I should rethink the whole thing and join the ministry that was established pursuant to the will of the Serb people there and that I should join the police and so on. So there were various attempts. But there was also this one that was rather provocative.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was this from an anonymous caller or from someone you knew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later on I learned who was behind this phone call. It was Mr. Dutina. Before the war, this man was a journalist, I believe, in "Oslobodjenje Daily" or perhaps on Sarajevo TV. I just know he was a media person. And whether at that time he was with the Government of Republika Srpska or not, I'm not sure, but I did learn eventually that this night-time call came from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the others who were trying to encourage you to join, can you recall by name who any of those were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Two friends of mine actually. The first was Vlastimir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- aka Vlasto, and the conversation he had with me was almost of military type. The other one was Slobodan Skipina, who was a very moderate man and very thoughtful, and he just sort of tried to tell me that I should try and see the whole picture, perhaps think it through, and then leave, together with my family, leave Sarajevo and join the forces of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is the interpreter says they didn't catch the last name of Vlastimir. Could you tell us that person's last name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlastimir Kusmuk, aka Vlasto.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Kusmuk was in the early days of the RS MUP, I think, the assistant minister heading up police administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then, I think, in August he was moved to be an advisor to the minister; did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the time when I had this black hole, you know, that was the time when I left the ministry, and at the time I didn't want to have anything to do with the Ministry of the Interior, so I can't really tell you with certainty that I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. You told us last Thursday at page 21396 that there came a point in time where you were not allowed into the MUP building in Sarajevo where you'd been working. Do you remember approximately how long after Mandic's dispatch was it that this happened? Was it a couple of days, was it a week, was it two weeks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the war had broken out and it was getting more and more difficult to leave Sarajevo, but certainly it was after the dispatch sent by Mr. Mandic, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned before that after you had taken your family out, you had either, I can't remember, is it on the way out you went through Trebinje or on the way coming back you went through Trebinje and had some problems because they seized your rental car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sabovic, Kemal, a friend, he suggested, and I followed his suggestion, and I took my two sons and my sister-in-law -- or daughter-in-law and his wife and their children, we rented a car from the Hertz rental agency at the Holiday Inn, we -- I took them to Trebinje where we spent the night at a football referee of the former Yugoslavia, Enver Saric, he was a referee in the former Yugoslavia, and he found accommodation for us in Herceg-Novi, in a studio apartment, I believe it was his brother's or another relative's, and I took -- when I took my children out, together with my mother-in-law, out of Sarajevo, that's where I took them. If you need me to go into more detail, I'm prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's enough. I want to ask you about that. When did you leave Trebinje to go back to the Sarajevo area, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would have had to be the first half of April, possibly around the 14th or 15th up to the 17th at the latest. I had a problem down there because members of the police station in Trebinje stopped my car. They asked for all the papers, the vehicle papers, everything. I had a contract, a rental contract. They confiscated the vehicle. And then a friend of mine let me use his own car, a Jetta Volkswagon, and I went to Sarajevo. And first I went through Serb barricades, then I entered Trnovo, then I went through Muslim barricades. And then on the approaches to Sarajevo, I, again, had to go to Serb barricades, and somehow I managed to get through. But this was sometime in mid-April, and that's what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have some documents in evidence about Trebinje and maybe some phone conversations that relate to that that can help us date it around mid-April. But where did you go precisely when you returned to Sarajevo then, after having taken your family to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take my family to Trebinje; I took them to Herceg-Novi. And I went back to my own apartment. In other words, I went back to the part of Sarajevo that was, let's put it that way, under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And precisely what part of town was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how well you know Sarajevo. That was in the part some one and a half kilometre to the south of the centre towards Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what police station boundary would that have been within?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the Novo Sarajevo Police Station where I was the commander, komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how long did you stay there and what were you doing? It must have been a difficult situation being a Serb and being in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a very difficult period. And not to repeat myself, but as I've already said, I spent most of my time in the apartment. And when I did go out, I would go out with a friend that I mentioned earlier, Kemal Sabovic. There was a cafe nearby and also Monik [phoen] Hotel, the owner of which was Alija Delimustafic, the then minister. So on two or three occasions I tried to get to the building. I've described that one occasion. Then on the second time, as I was passing by Hotel Zagreb, I was intercepted by a criminal from Bascarsija who wore some kind of uniform and had a weapon. It wasn't a very hostile meeting, but he did suggest that I leave Sarajevo, and he told me that if I could not manage to do that, that he would help me get out of the city. And he said, You know, there are many people in this town who would be glad to soak in your blood. And then I tried -- the third occasion was when I tried to return the car to my friend Dragan Djurovic. The vehicle was taken be -- confiscated by Jusuf Razina [phoen] it was a new Peugeot vehicle parked outside the police club in Sarajevo. So this was a very unpleasant situation because none of these people - there were a couple of people there that I knew - none of them were willing to talk to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand from your earlier testimony that there came a point in time, then, when you left that part of town and you went to Ilidza. Pardon my pronunciation. When was that approximately? How many days had you been back before you went to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I really can't recall the date exactly or when it was that I went to Ilidza. But I recall there was a convoy of children that was -- that headed from Sarajevo to -- toward the coast or somewhere inland, and it was stopped. I recall that very well because I was stopped and a member of Arkan's unit asked me for my papers. I remember that I had to get out of the car. But I can't recall the exact date, but it must have been around May already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When -- I'm sorry, why did you decide to go to Ilidza? What was your reason for going there, what was your plan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned that perhaps a day before I left there was a very unpleasant search that was carried out by a paramilitary unit headed by a certain Rus [phoen]. This was a very unpleasant search. It was brutal, even vulgar. And that night, I believe, I received a phone call from an honourable man, and I think I've mentioned that his name was Dr. Nakes [phoen], and he told me that the best option for me, because he had learned some information from someone, would be to leave Sarajevo as soon as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I certainly understand your reasons for leaving. My question is more to: Why was Ilidza the place you decided to go? Why there instead of Trebinje or Herceg-Novi or somewhere else? Why Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because most of my friends were in Ilidza. That's where I had grown up. My sister also lived there, she had an apartment there, so I decided to go to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us that when you got there you had some contact with Mr. Tomo Kovac. Did you know him before this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to the police station at Ilidza. I'm not certain anymore whether in a conversation with Kusmuk or Skipina, but one of them probably mentioned a name who it was that I should go and see if I were to leave Sarajevo, so I did. I went to Ilidza and I reported to Mr. Kovac, who was at the station, and I knew that man. I had known him from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was your nature of knowing him from before? How long had you known him and what was the nature of your acquaintance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a little later, perhaps in 1978, he too started working with the state security service. And there was a special department there that only did background checks for individuals, and he was employed, he worked there, in that department. I don't know how long he stayed there. We were never very close, but we were colleagues. We were co-workers. What I'm trying to say is we never socialised privately. But I know that when I was appointed commander of the police station in Novo Sarajevo, Jozo Leotar was the commander of the Novi Grad Police Station, and I believe that at this time Mr. Kovac was his deputy in Novi Grad. I can't recall whether that was before or after the Olympic Games, but what I do know for a fact is that he was the deputy to Mr. Jozo Leotar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on Thursday, at page 21399, you told us while there in Ilidza that Mr. Kovac made you an offer that you stay there and work as his deputy but that you refused "because before the war, during the war, and after the war, I did not agree with some of his ideas and thoughts." My question, Mr. Andan, is, What ideas and thoughts of Tomo Kovac did you not agree with that caused you to decline his offer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are many causes there, and I'll try to be brief and tell you what my main reason was and why it was that I declined his offer to be his deputy at Ilidza. First of all, based on my background and my career, I was always his superior. And to be honest with you, I felt it was humiliating to be his subordinate now, especially so because he said that I would be his deputy and on those days they were preparing an operation on Stup. And the Stup was the place where my parents were living at the time, and I told him, You know, I don't think that's right, I don't think -- my parents are living there, and I don't think it would be fair because if anything should go wrong, if anything should happen, I would be left without my parents. Now, the main bone of contention, as it were, with him was an investigation that was conducted while he was the deputy commander in Novi Grad, where in Ilijas he bought from Mr. Ibro Muslic. There was a company there that dealt in rented vehicles, the sales of rented vehicles, and I know that there was something untoward happening there. He was involved in some kind of under-the-table deal. And I went there, I tried to help him. And I asked Mr. Ibro Muslic to return the vehicle so that we don't have to -- so that we don't have to initiate disciplinary proceedings. And when I came back, I told him that Mr. Muslic had agreed to return this vehicle. It was a Kadett Opel vehicle. But at first he was very indignant. He said, you know, Who gave you the right to do this? And so on. But later on he was -- actually, some friends of his actually agreed with my position. They told him, you know, he was right in doing this. This was the right course of action. And because of these dealings of his and that kind of conduct, I did not even want to be in the same building where he was. And as I've already said, there were Kijac and Mandic and all these other men that I mentioned earlier, they were in his office when I got there, so that's the reason why I didn't even want to go there and see him. Now, later on, as Mr. Kovac was a very vengeful man and a careerist, he thought that I would be a threat to his further promotion in service, and he tried, even after the war, to sort of eliminate me by even filing some false complaints charging me with things that I had even ordered his execution and so on. So in brief, this is the person that Mr. Kovac was. And I really don't even want to talk about him because I dislike even the thought or the name when I hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I do want to ask you one more question about him, then, though. Didn't he, after the war, at some point in time, go so far as to make a written complaint about you and allege that you and Mico Davidovic had tried to kill him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he filed a complaint to the lower prosecutor's office in Bijeljina that allegedly I had ordered his execution through the Zemun clan, a clan, a criminal clan, and of course I just decline to even talk about that, refuse to even discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that there's no truth to that, that you and Mico Davidovic did anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis, the part of the answer of the witness was not recorded, and I believe it will be helpful for your next question. Because he explained what was done with that complaint, that it went to court, and so on and so forth. So maybe he can repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, you heard what was said just then. Can you elaborate for us a little; there actually was a complaint filed in criminal court and what happened with those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what happened before the criminal complaint, based on what I learned, I can tell you about that, too. At the time, I was the director of police of Republika Srpska, and at the time we were beginning to deal with the crimes that had been committed during the war. In other words, we began dealing with war profiteers. And Mr. Kovac was frightened that he might become the focus of the police investigation, so he tried to pre-empt our investigation by submitting a criminal complaint to the lower prosecutor's office in Bijeljina in which he charged me with attempting, with the assistance of some criminals from the Zemun clan, of trying to organise his execution. And I tried -- I was actually questioned and interviewed at the lower prosecutor's office in Bijeljina, and after a while I learned that the criminal complaint that Mr. Tomislav Kovac had filed against me was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We do understand that there were attempts made to have investigations made into the commission of war crimes, but I think you should sharpen your focus and speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am going to move on to another one now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- at page 21399, line 24, on Thursday you told us that after declining the offer in Ilidza, that you went to Vraca. How did you come to go there? Did somebody send you there? Or did somebody request you to go there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the initial interview with Mr. Kovac in the police station in Ilidza, after my offer was refused, he asked me where I was accommodated. I told him that I was staying with my sister at Ilidza. He told me to come again in several days. He said that he would contact the ministry, which was at Pale at the time, and they would probably decide where to send me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then what happened? How did you get to Vraca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept reporting to Mr. Kovac. I spent seven or maybe even ten days in Ilidza. One day when I arrived there, he told me that his vehicle or a MUP vehicle from Ilidza was going to go to Vraca and that they were going to transfer me to the police school in Vraca. After that, I was supposed to receive instructions about what to do next. And that's what happened. We went to the airport. The airport was closed at the time. And that's when I finally ended up in Vraca in the police school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did you report to when you got there and what were you told to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Milos Zuban was there. The way I understood it at the time, he was chief of the police administration, maybe even chief of a department. I know that I reported to him. He told me that I could reside in a room where Mr. Mihajlo Bajic was. He told me that he would inform the ministry at Pale that I was there and that they would see where I was going to be assigned later. So I spent the period of time at Vraca. I'm unable to tell you exactly how long. I simply went to breakfast, lunch, and dinner every day, I spent the rest of the time in the room, and I had no assignments whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us on Thursday right at the end of the day that you'd had some problem with the Serbs even before arriving in Vraca, but I guess also upon arriving there, because they had questions about why did you stay so long in Sarajevo in the old MUP, why did you leave so late. Some of them were concerned that you might be a spy for the Muslims. Is that part of the reason that you weren't getting any assignment for a while after you arrived in Vraca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was attacked, under quotation marks, by those who went first to fight among the Serbs, by those who did not use their head to think with it. I have to go back now and mention the thoughts of some people who tried to figure out whether they needed me or not. I definitely was needed to perform some police duties, while other people thought that I would be promoted very soon and they would end up being my inferiors. Yes, there were provocations. People kept asking whether I was there -- why I was there for such a long time; whether I was infiltrated by Alija's services; whether I was a Serb at all or not, and if was, what kind of a Serb I was. So I managed to sail through all that and I really tried during that period of time to spend most of the time with Mijhalo Bajic. He was about ten years older than I was, and we played chess and discussed various topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, where are we going with all of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to get through the chronology that was presented the Defence case, and I have other arguments that will relate to this chronology. I ask your patience for a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Unless you have an urgent point relating to the indictment, I think you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand, Your Honour, but, at the same time, at the end of the case I have to make submissions, Prosecution has to make submissions, about the evidence, about the credibility of the witnesses, about the weight to give testimony of witnesses and the physical evidence, and some of this is important for that because this witness will be an important witness for both sides, and that's why I ask your indulgence. But my next question will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Hannis, let me just make it clear to you that I don't find any of your questions going to the credibility of the witness, nor do I see the relevance to any point in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think this is an appropriate time for me to make my arguments about how this relates to his credibility, but I promise you that I have a plan and an intention and a reason for asking these questions that I'm asking and the order in which I'm asking that will go to the argument at the end. And if you want me to have the witness leave the room and explain to you in further detail, I'm willing to do that, but my next question is:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you get an assignment? Who gave it to you? And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said, I think Mr. Skipina told me, that there were discussions about my future engagements and that Mr. Stanisic cut the chase and said that I'm a person which could be used by the ministry at the time. And then he asked what was the most difficult assignment in the territory of Republika Srpska at the time, somebody said Brcko, and a proposal was made for me to be sent to Brcko so that I could solve the problems there and thereby show that I know how to do my job. So my assignment was to go to Pale, where I received further instructions, and after that I went towards Bijeljina with Danilo Vukovic. I think I described that in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that remark by Mr. Stanisic was not something you heard directly from him but was reported to you by Mr. Skipina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Slobo told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And even though you've gotten this important job in Brcko, were you provided a car to get there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not given a car. I told you already that I was told to go to the police station in Kula and to get a car from Mr Tepavcevic. He was not prepared to give me a vehicle at that moment, so we were transported by a series of police cars from police station to police station, from Pale to Sokolac, from Sokolac to Han Pijesak, and so on until Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us about your arrival in Bijeljina encounter with Mr. Devedlaka who told you you should flee, as he apparently was doing the same, and then you reported I think a day or two later to Mr. Jesuric, Predrag Jesuric. What was his position at the time in Bijeljina, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be a problem in interpretation; it wasn't Mr. Jasarevic. Let me tell you straightaway, Mr. Devedlaka didn't suggest, he urged us to flee from Bijeljina. That's what he said. After one or two days, we called -- we were called to the police station in Bijeljina, a vehicle came to pick us up, that vehicle transported us to Bijeljina, and we reported to Mr. Predrag Jesuric. He was the chief there, and we reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say he was the chief. Was he the chief of the SJB or the CSB or both? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the chief of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what task or assignment did he give you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already stated, before the war there would always be two policemen who perform supervisory inspection. My assignment that I received in Pale was to go and perform supervisory inspection and provide professional and other assistance in police stations. He separated us. He said that Danilo Vukovic was supposed to go to Zvornik and that I should go to Brcko. So in addition to the basic work that I had to do, because it was part of my job, I was also supposed to assist in the establishment of the police station in Brcko. That was the context of the dispatch of Mr. Jesuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 1D547.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Andan, while's that's coming up --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this was a Defence exhibit dated 1st or 2nd June. Yeah, it's tab 83 in the Prosecution list, tab 15 in the Defence list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your testimony about this document and what you were doing on your first days in Brcko, a few times you said "we," as in the plural, and were -- and I had the impression that you were with Danilo Vukovic, but I understand he was given a different task. So were you the only inspector there, or was there someone else helping you do that inspection job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said quite clearly that Danilo Vukovic went to Zvornik while I went to Brcko. I was the only inspector in Brcko. However, when I say "we," I refer to the management of the police station. I was not superior to the chief of the police station. My task there was to perform supervisory inspection and provide all assistance required from me. So I could propose to the chief various measures that he could introduce in order to consolidate the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you first got there, to Brcko, did you have a one-on-one meeting with the chief before this meeting with the specialist board?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by "specialist board," but of course I had to carry out an informative conversation with the chief, because, you know, when you come into somebody's house, first you talk to the host of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That makes sense. That's why I ask. And I assume that's what you did. When I said "specialist board," I'm just reading from this document which says "minutes of the meeting of the specialist board of the Serb SJB." So that's where I picked up the term. It's on the document in my English translation. Do you have it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the management of the police station. A fully complemented police station has commander, his deputy, and his assistants, and they comprise the collegium of the police station. There is also a chief of the crime prevention service and, if necessary, the chief of the civilian affairs. So this is the collegium of the management of a police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that Mr. Veselic, who was the chief at this time, had been appointed, I guess, after the bridges on the Sava River were blown up in Brcko. And we established, I think, that that happened on the 30th of April, 1992. Do you know or do you remember who had been the chief of the SJB in Brcko before the bridges were blown up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, even about what you just said, that is, that he had been appointed -- that he was appointed chief after the bridges were blown up. So I'm not sure. He may have been appointed before that event. I don't know. And I also don't know who was the chief of the police station in Brcko before the bridges were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned that a few days after you were there you had some problems with some of Captain Dragan's men led by a certain Rane. Can you tell the Judges what you know about Captain Dragan; who was he and who were his men that were in the Brcko area at this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must be some problem in interpretation again. It was wasn't "Rane"; it was a "Rade." They were members of a paramilitary formation that was trained and sent to the territory of Republika Srpska by Captain Dragan. That's what I know. They weren't part of any armed forces of Yugoslavia or police forces of Serbia and Montenegro. To my mind, it was a paramilitary formation, and he was a person who trained and sent paramilitary formations. So this trail went from Brcko towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know who he was, where he was from, his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I can't remember, although I do know his first and last name. He is from Serbia, of course. As far as I know, when the war began in the former Yugoslavia, he arrived in Serbia from Australia. Then I think he was in Knin, where he also organised some sort of paramilitary formations, Red Berets, and then as the war spread, he also began operating in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. His first name is Dragan and I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before this meeting that's reflected in the document on the screen in front of you, in your meeting with Chief Veselic, had he briefed you about the situation in Brcko and what had happened since the bridges were blown at the end of April? What had he told you about the security situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR ANDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to talk to a person who did not belong to the same profession. His first job in the Ministry of the Interior was the job that he had in Brcko. Then, at the time, he tried to explain to me various positions of units around Brcko, and he almost did not talk about the problems in the police station, which, as I told you, was not functioning at the time. I posed the questions that are normal when somebody arrives in the police station for the first time. I wanted to know the level of the manpower, their qualifications, and similar things. Well, he did not know the answers to those questions. He made no effort to prepare for the meeting. He said that they had problems, that they did not have policemen, that the military took all the policemen and used them at the front line. He also said that they had the problem with the paramilitary formations and that they did not know what to do about it. He said that this was a pronounced problem. It is quite clear that at the time he did not have enough courage to re-organise the station in order to resolve the problem on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honours. I think we'll stop here for the day, Mr. Andan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment to resume -- [Microphone not activated] We resume in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
